backTranslations.41:
**Before the appointment**
- Enter the appointment date on the Doctor tab. MenoMap shows how ready your notes are and what would make them stronger.
- Choose the most important topics and questions. Three or four is enough.
- Prepare your notes for the last 30 or 90 days. Check that your medication list is up to date.

**At the appointment**
- Hand over or show the first page. It was made so it can be read in a minute: numbers, averages, the heat calendar and your questions.
- Start with the question that matters most to you.
- If your doctor speaks another language, you can prepare the notes in that language too.

**What the notes are and are not**

They summarize what you recorded and whatever you decided to bring in from the Health app. They do not represent a diagnosis or complete medical documentation, and the patterns in them are coincidence checks, not proof of the cause. Your doctor may ask questions the notes do not answer, and that is completely normal.

**After the appointment**

Add new medications with their start date. After a few weeks MenoMap can show your entries before and after, which makes the next review easier.
backTranslations.42:
**Menopause** is a single point in time: the day when you have already gone 12 consecutive months without a period, and no other cause explains it (for example pregnancy, certain medications or surgery). In many countries it occurs on average in the early 50s, but anywhere from the mid-40s to the mid-50s is common.

**Perimenopause** is the stage of the years before that point. Hormone levels rise and fall unevenly, so periods can become irregular, heavier or lighter, and come more or less often. Many changes people associate with menopause, such as hot flashes, night sweats, and changes in sleep and mood, often start already then, while there are still periods. Perimenopause can last a few years or considerably longer, and it goes differently for everyone.

**Postmenopause** is everything that follows after the 12-month mark. Some symptoms ease over time, others can persist for years.

Menopause can also occur earlier because of surgery removing the ovaries, certain anti-cancer treatments or other illnesses. Menopause before age 40 is sometimes called premature ovarian insufficiency, and it is worth discussing with a doctor.

**How it is recognized.** In many people over 45, the doctor recognizes perimenopause or menopause from the history and symptoms. A blood test is not always needed, because hormone levels fluctuate from day to day. It is done rather when someone is younger or the picture is not clear.

**What MenoMap does and does not do.** MenoMap cannot tell you which stage you are in. What it can do: honestly record what you notice – flashes, sleep, mood and treatment – so that you and your doctor see the same picture.

backTranslations.162:
Doctors call hot flashes and night sweats **vasomotor symptoms**. A hot flash is a sudden feeling of heat, often on the face, neck and chest, sometimes with flushing, sweating, a racing heartbeat or chills afterwards. Night sweats are the same during sleep, and can be so strong that you wake from it or your bedding gets soaked.

They are among the most common changes around menopause. Some people get only a few mild ones, others many a day, which disrupts work and sleep. For some they pass within a few years, for others they last much longer.

**What can make them more likely.** Many people notice a connection with alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, warm rooms, stress or thick bedding. These differ greatly from person to person, so tracking your own labels can be more useful than a general list.

**There can be other causes.** Flushing and sweating can also be caused by thyroid problems, infections, certain medications, anxiety and other illnesses. If your symptoms do not fit the usual pattern, or come with weight loss, fever or feeling unwell, tell a doctor.

**How to describe them well.** Useful details for the appointment:
- Roughly how many occur during the day and at night
- How strong they are and how long they last
- What they interrupt: sleep, work, conversation, exercise
- What tends to precede them
- What you have already tried and whether it changed anything

MenoMap's Flash button and retrospective log are made for recording exactly this, without much effort.

**Help exists.** There are hormonal and non-hormonal treatment options, and practical solutions. Which one suits you is worth discussing with a doctor.

backTranslations.291:
Hormone replacement therapy (often also called HRT or MHT) replaces some of the estrogen that the body produces less of around menopause. According to the main professional guidelines, for many people it is an effective treatment for hot flashes and night sweats, and it can help with other symptoms too.

**It has different forms:** patches, gels, sprays, tablets, and low-dose vaginal preparations for local symptoms such as dryness. For someone who still has her uterus, a progestogen is usually prescribed alongside the estrogen to protect the uterine lining.

**The benefits and risks differ from person to person:** they depend on age, on how much time has passed since periods stopped, on your own and family history (for example breast cancer, blood clots, stroke or heart disease), and on the type and delivery method of the treatment. So this is a decision to be made with a doctor who knows your history, and not something an app can decide.

**Frequently asked questions:**
- Is hormone replacement therapy an option for me, and why or why not?
- What type and form would you recommend, and why?
- What benefits can I expect, and how soon?
- What are my personal risks, and how do they compare with not being treated?
- What should I watch for, and when should we review it again?

**If you are already taking it,** record it in MenoMap (Profile → Medications). MenoMap shows your flashes before and after starting the treatment, as a coincidence check, not proof, so there is something tangible you can discuss at the review.

MenoMap never recommends starting, stopping or changing a medication.

backTranslations.293:
Hormone replacement therapy is not right for everyone, and some people would simply choose another path. There are several of these.

**Prescription options.** For some non-hormonal medications there is evidence that they reduce hot flashes. These include certain medications originally developed for other illnesses, and a newer group of medications developed specifically for hot flashes. Each has its own benefits, side effects and interactions, so a doctor can help weigh them.

**Talk-based and mind-body methods.** For cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) tailored to menopause there is evidence that it makes hot flashes and night sweats less bothersome, and improves sleep. Clinical hypnosis has also been studied.

**Practical changes that many people find helpful:**
- Layers that can be taken off quickly
- A fan on the desk and beside the bed
- A cooler bedroom and well-ventilated bedding
- Recognizing and reducing your personal triggers (MenoMap's labels and experiments help with this)
- Regular exercise and a steady sleep routine

**Supplements and herbal preparations.** Many of them have mixed or limited evidence, their quality varies, and some interact with other medications. Tell your doctor or pharmacist everything you take, including over-the-counter preparations.

**Try one change at a time.** MenoMap's two-week experiments compare your own entries before and during a change, which is easier to judge than a feeling.

backTranslations.416:
Most medical appointments are short, and it is hard to recall a month of nights on the spot. People tend to remember the most recent or the worst days. A simple record fills this gap.

**What a diary gives your doctor:**
- How often symptoms occur and how strong they are, not just that they exist
- Whether they are improving, worsening or unchanged
- What happened around them: sleep, alcohol, stress, medications
- A baseline to compare against if you try a treatment

**Keep it light.** A diary only helps if you keep it. MenoMap is built on a one-tap Flash button and a four-question evening questionnaire, so it takes seconds, no notebook needed.

**Two weeks is a good start.** Two to four weeks of entries usually gives a clearer picture than a single bad week.

**Bring your questions too.** Write down what matters most to you: which symptom bothers you most, what you would like to try or avoid, and what worries you. MenoMap's Doctor tab helps choose the questions, and prints them together with your notes.

backTranslations.479:
If you have gone 12 months without a period, **any vaginal bleeding must be checked by a doctor**, even if it happened only once, and even if it was only spotting or a pale pink or brown discharge.

In most cases the cause is not serious. Common, for example, is thinning of the lining of the vagina or the uterus. However, post-menopausal bleeding can sometimes be an early sign of a condition that is much easier to treat when found early. That is why, according to public health recommendations, it must be checked, and one should not wait with it.

**If you use hormone replacement therapy,** certain bleeding patterns are expected depending on the type of treatment. If the bleeding is unexpected relative to your treatment, heavier than usual or does not come at the right time, that too must be checked.

**What to do:**
- Turn to your doctor or your healthcare provider, and tell them that you have had post-menopausal bleeding.
- Note the date, the amount and anything else you noticed. MenoMap keeps this for you (Profile → Cycle).

MenoMap cannot tell why the bleeding happened. It will remind you to have it checked, and includes it in your appointment notes.

backTranslations.529:
Poor sleep is one of the most common complaints of midlife, and it rarely has a single cause.

**Night sweats** can wake you directly, or leave you too hot and damp to fall asleep again.

**Other common factors:**
- Urge to urinate at night
- Anxiety or racing thoughts
- Alcohol, which can help you fall asleep but often makes sleep fragmented in the second half of the night
- Caffeine later in the day
- Pain, restless legs or a partner's snoring
- Snoring or pauses in breathing, which can be a sign of sleep apnea (worth bringing up, especially if you are very sleepy during the day)

**What helps many people.** A cool, dark room; well-ventilated bedding and removable layers; a steady wake-up time; and less alcohol before bed. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured, well-studied method, and many doctors can refer you to it.

**What is worth tracking.** For one or two weeks note your sleep score, night flashes, alcohol and late caffeine. MenoMap's evening questionnaire and flash log do this in a few taps. If you use an Apple Watch, MenoMap also shows your sleep and wrist temperature from the Health app alongside night sweats, as background information, not as an explanation.

**When to ask for an evaluation.** Talk to a doctor if poor sleep affects your safety (for example while driving), your mood or your daily life, or if you notice pauses in breathing or gasping for air at night.
